newsitem.title: USA: Guidant says FDA clears broader catheter label.
newsitem.headline: Guidant says FDA clears broader catheter label.

text.p: Guidant Corp said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved expanded product labeling for its balloon dilatation catheters to include angioplasty for the treatment of heart attack.
Guidant said it is the only balloon dilatation catheter maker to receive the expanded labeling for a heart attack indication.

"The FDA's decision to recognize PTCA (percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty) as an effective first-time treatment for heart attack is an important step in educating physicians about the value of treating heart attack patients with angioplasty," said Ginger Howard, president of Guidant's vascular intervention group.

The new labeling is based on data from the Global Use of Strategies to Open Occluded Arteries II, or GUSTO IIb, sub-study, which showed that balloon angioplasty is a more effective treatment than clot-busting drugs when used immediately following a heart attack, Guidant said.
The GUSTO II study, led by investigators from the Cleveland Clinic and Duke University, was a worldwide study to examine treatments for heart attacks, also known as acute myocardial infarction.

One portion of the study, involving more than 1,100 patients, compared the effectiveness of balloon angioplasty to the accelerated use of the clot-busting drug t-PA in opening blocked coronary arteries, Guidant said.

The research found that at 30 days, patients undergoing angioplasty were 30 percent less likely to die, and less likely to experience a repeat heart attack or disabling stroke than those treated with t-PA, made by Genentech Inc and marketed under the name Activase.
At six months and again at one year there was no statistical difference noted, Guidant said.

"Direct angioplasty, when it can be accomplished on a prompt basis by experienced physicians at centers with catheterization laboratory availability, should be considered a primary treatment option for patients with acute myocardial infarction," Guidant said.
Guidant's vascular intervention group provided technical consultation, financial support and the majority of balloon catheters used in the independently managed sub-study.
